source.text: וַיַּ֥עַן אִיּ֗וֹב וַיֹּאמַֽר׃

records.literal_gloss: And answered Job and said:

en.L: And Job answered and said:
en.B: Then Job replied:
en.R: Then Job answered:

decisions.choice: answered and said: the formula that opens a speech
decisions.reason: "He answered and said" introduces each speech in the dialogue (4:1; 8:1; 9:1). It marks a reply in the debate, here Job's answer to Eliphaz (chapters 4-5).
Balanced and Readable use one verb for the Hebrew pair. Literal keeps both. The line is prose, not poetry.

source.text: ל֗וּ שָׁק֣וֹל יִשָּׁקֵ֣ל כַּעְשִׂ֑י וְ֝הַוָּתִ֗י בְּֽמֹאזְנַ֥יִם יִשְׂאוּ־יָֽחַד׃

records.literal_gloss: If only actually were weighed my vexation, and my calamity in [the] scales they would lift together!

en.L: If only my vexation were truly weighed, \q and my calamity lifted onto [the] scales together!
en.B: If only my anguish could be weighed \q and all my calamity laid on the scales!
en.R: I wish someone could weigh my pain \q and put all my troubles on a scale!

decisions.choice: my vexation: Job takes up Eliphaz's word
decisions.reason: Eliphaz warned that ka'as, brooding anger, kills the fool (5:2). Job answers with the same word: if his ka'as were weighed, it would be found to have a cause.

decisions.choice: my calamity, as the scribes' reading has it
decisions.reason: The written consonants (ketiv) and the reading the scribes marked (qere) spell this word differently, with one letter changed; the scribes' reading is the word for calamity or ruin, which Job uses again in 6:30.
Lu ("if only") with the verb doubled ("weighing, it were weighed") makes an urgent wish: if only it could really be weighed.
"Together" means all of it at once; Balanced and Readable say "all".

source.text: כִּֽי־עַתָּ֗ה מֵח֣וֹל יַמִּ֣ים יִכְבָּ֑ד עַל־כֵּ֝֗ן דְּבָרַ֥י לָֽעוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: For now than [the] sand of [the] seas it would be heavy; therefore my words have been rash.

en.L: For now it would be heavier than [the] sand of [the] seas; \q therefore my words have been rash.
en.B: For now it would outweigh the sand of the seas; \q that is why my words have been wild.
en.R: It would be heavier than all the sand of the sea. \q That is why I have spoken so wildly.

decisions.reason: La'u is a rare verb, probably related to a word for speaking wildly (Proverbs 20:25). Job admits his words in chapter 3 were extreme, and says the weight of his suffering explains them.

decisions.choice: the sand of the seas: past all measuring
decisions.reason: The sand of the sea stands for what cannot be counted or carried (Genesis 22:17; Proverbs 27:3).
Readable makes Job the subject of the sentence.

source.text: כִּ֤י חִצֵּ֪י שַׁדַּ֡י עִמָּדִ֗י אֲשֶׁ֣ר חֲ֭מָתָם שֹׁתָ֣ה רוּחִ֑י בִּעוּתֵ֖י אֱל֣וֹהַּ יַֽעַרְכֽוּנִי׃

records.literal_gloss: For [the] arrows of [the] Almighty [are] with me, whose poison drinks my spirit; [the] terrors of God are arrayed against me.

en.L: For [the] arrows of the Almighty [are] in me, \q whose poison my spirit drinks; \q [the] terrors of God are arrayed against me.
en.B: For the arrows of the Almighty are in me, \q and my spirit drinks their poison; \q the terrors of God are lined up against me.
en.R: God All-Powerful has shot {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} arrows into me, \q and their poison is soaking into my spirit. \q God's terrors are lined up against me like an army.

decisions.choice: the arrows of the Almighty: suffering sent by God
decisions.reason: God's arrows are a picture of the pain he sends (Deuteronomy 32:23; Psalm 38:3; Lamentations 3:12-13). Job does not doubt who is behind his suffering; Eliphaz said God wounds and heals (5:18), and Job feels only the wound.
Ruach can be wind, breath or spirit. Here it is the inner person, which the poison soaks into.

decisions.choice: arrayed against me: drawn up for battle
decisions.reason: The verb is used of an army drawn up in battle lines (1 Samuel 17:8; Judges 20:22). God's terrors stand ranked against Job like soldiers.
Readable's usual name for Shaddai (5:17).
Readable makes the military picture explicit (m3).

source.text: הֲיִֽנְהַק־פֶּ֥רֶא עֲלֵי־דֶ֑שֶׁא אִ֥ם יִגְעֶה־שּׁ֝֗וֹר עַל־בְּלִילֽוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: Does bray a wild donkey over fresh grass, or does low an ox over its fodder?

en.L: Does a wild donkey bray over grass? \q Or does an ox low over its fodder?
en.B: Does a wild donkey bray when it has grass, \q or an ox bellow over its feed?
en.R: A wild donkey does not cry out when it has grass to eat, \q and an ox does not complain when it has food.

decisions.choice: questions expecting the answer "no": animals cry out only when they lack something
decisions.reason: A wild donkey or an ox that has food is quiet. Job means that his cries, too, have a cause: he is not complaining for nothing.
Belil is feed made from mixed grain and chaff (Isaiah 30:24).
Readable gives the answer the questions expect (m1), which is easier to follow.

source.text: הֲיֵאָכֵ֣ל תָּ֭פֵל מִבְּלִי־מֶ֑לַח אִם־יֶשׁ־טַ֝֗עַם בְּרִ֣יר חַלָּמֽוּת׃

records.literal_gloss: Is eaten tasteless [food] without salt, or is there taste in [the] slime of purslane?

en.L: Is tasteless [food] eaten without salt? \q Or is there taste in [the] slime of purslane?
en.B: Can tasteless food be eaten without salt, \q or is there any flavor in the slime of purslane?
en.R: Who can eat bland food without salt? \q Is there any taste in the slimy juice of a weed?

decisions.choice: the slime of purslane: the slimy juice of a plant
decisions.reason: Challamut appears only here. It may be a plant with slimy juice, such as purslane or mallow; an old Jewish tradition took the phrase as the white of an egg. Either way it is something with no taste.

decisions.choice: what is tasteless: Eliphaz's advice, or Job's suffering
decisions.reason: Job does not say what the tasteless food stands for. It may be the comfort Eliphaz has offered, which Job cannot swallow, or the suffering he is made to eat. Verse 7 says he refuses to touch it.
Readable names the kind of plant rather than a name few readers know.

source.text: מֵאֲנָ֣ה לִנְגּ֣וֹעַ נַפְשִׁ֑י הֵ֝֗מָּה כִּדְוֵ֥י לַחְמִֽי׃

records.literal_gloss: Refuses to touch [them] my soul; they [are] like [the] sickness of my food.

en.L: My soul refuses to touch [them]; \q they [are] like sickness [in] my food.
en.B: I refuse to touch them; \q they are like food that makes me sick.
en.R: I will not even touch such food; \q it makes me sick.

decisions.choice: my soul: I myself, my appetite
decisions.reason: Nefesh is the self, and often the appetite or throat (Proverbs 27:7). "My soul refuses" means "I cannot bring myself".

decisions.choice: like sickness in my food: food that disgusts
alternatives: they are my food when I am sick
my food is like something diseased
decisions.reason: The line is hard, and the words can be joined in more than one way. The likely sense is that these things are as loathsome to Job as spoiled food.
Balanced and Readable say "I" for nefesh here (m1). Literal keeps "my soul".

source.text: מִֽי־יִ֭תֵּן תָּב֣וֹא שֶֽׁאֱלָתִ֑י וְ֝תִקְוָתִ֗י יִתֵּ֥ן אֱלֽוֹהַּ׃

records.literal_gloss: Who will give [that] my request come, and my hope God would grant?

en.L: Who will grant [that] my request come, \q and [that] God give [me] my hope?
en.B: Oh, that my request would be granted, \q that God would give me what I hope for:
en.R: How I wish I could have what I ask for, \q that God would give me what I long for:

decisions.choice: who will give: a way of saying "if only"
decisions.reason: Mi yitten ("who will give") introduces a wish, not a question (Job 14:13; 19:23).

decisions.choice: my hope: Job's only hope now is death
decisions.reason: Eliphaz told Job that his hope should be his integrity (4:6). Job's answer is bitter: the only hope he has left is that God will end his life (verse 9).

decisions.choice: the verse ends with a colon
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable make the wish one sentence with verse 9, which says what Job asks for.

source.text: וְיֹאֵ֣ל אֱ֭לוֹהַּ וִֽידַכְּאֵ֑נִי יַתֵּ֥ר יָ֝ד֗וֹ וִֽיבַצְּעֵֽנִי׃

records.literal_gloss: And may be willing God and crush me, may he loosen his hand and cut me off!

en.L: And [that] God would be willing and crush me, \q let loose {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} hand and cut me off!
en.B: that God would be willing to crush me, \q to let loose {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} hand and cut me off!
en.R: that God would decide to crush me, \q to reach out {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} hand and end my life!

decisions.choice: loosen his hand: no longer hold it back
decisions.reason: God's hand is pictured as held back; Job wants him to let it go and strike. In the prologue God limited what the accuser could do to Job (1:12; 2:6); Job wants God's hand free.

decisions.choice: cut me off: end my life
decisions.reason: Batsa' is to cut off, as a weaver cuts the finished cloth from the loom (Isaiah 38:12).

decisions.choice: Job asks God for death; he does not take his own life
decisions.reason: Job wants God to end his life, but he leaves the deed to God. He never curses God, as the accuser said he would (1:11; 2:5).
Readable says plainly what the picture means (m2).

source.text: וּ֥תְהִי ע֨וֹד׀נֶ֘חָ֤מָתִ֗י וַאֲסַלְּדָ֣ה בְ֭חִילָה לֹ֣א יַחְמ֑וֹל כִּי־לֹ֥א כִ֝חַ֗דְתִּי אִמְרֵ֥י קָדֽוֹשׁ׃

records.literal_gloss: And may it still be my comfort, and I would leap in anguish [that] does not spare, that not I have hidden [the] words of [the] Holy One.

en.L: Then it would still be my comfort, \q and I would leap [for joy] in pain [that] does not spare, \q that I have not hidden [the] words of the Holy One.
en.B: Then I would still have this comfort, \q and I would leap for joy in pain that does not let up: \q that I have not denied the words of the Holy One.
en.R: Then I would still have one comfort, \q and I would jump for joy even in pain that never stops: \q I have never turned away from what the Holy One said.

decisions.reason: The verb is found only here. It probably means to leap or exult. Some take it as "recoil" or "stand firm" in pain. Job's comfort, either way, is that he dies faithful.
To hide words is to deny or suppress them (Psalm 40:11; Isaiah 3:9). Job has not turned his back on what God commanded.
"The Holy One" is a title for God, especially in the prophets (Isaiah 40:25; Hosea 11:9). It is the only time Job uses it.
"Does not spare" most likely describes the pain, which shows no pity; it could also mean that God does not spare Job.
The verb means to leap (m1); "for joy" is supplied to show why. Literal brackets it.

source.text: מַה־כֹּחִ֥י כִֽי־אֲיַחֵ֑ל וּמַה־קִּ֝צִּ֗י כִּֽי־אַאֲרִ֥יךְ נַפְשִֽׁי׃

records.literal_gloss: What [is] my strength, that I should wait, and what [is] my end, that I should prolong my soul?

en.L: What [is] my strength, that I should wait? \q And what [is] my end, that I should be patient?
en.B: What strength do I have, that I should keep waiting? \q What future do I have, that I should be patient?
en.R: Do I have the strength to keep on waiting? \q What do I have to look forward to, that I should be patient?

decisions.reason: To lengthen one's soul is to be patient, to hold out; the opposite, a soul grown short, means impatience (Numbers 21:4; Judges 16:16).

decisions.choice: my end: the outcome, what lies ahead
decisions.reason: Qets is an end or outcome. Job has nothing to wait for.
Every level gives the sense of the idiom (m1), since "prolong my soul" says nothing in English.

source.text: אִם־כֹּ֣חַ אֲבָנִ֣ים כֹּחִ֑י אִֽם־בְּשָׂרִ֥י נָחֽוּשׁ׃

records.literal_gloss: Is [the] strength of stones my strength? Or [is] my flesh bronze?

en.L: Is my strength [the] strength of stones? \q Or [is] my flesh bronze?
en.B: Is my strength the strength of stone? \q Is my flesh made of bronze?
en.R: Am I as strong as stone? \q Is my body made of bronze?

decisions.reason: Job is not made of stone or metal; he cannot endure without end.
Basar here is Job's body, which is already afflicted (2:7).

source.text: הַאִ֬ם אֵ֣ין עֶזְרָתִ֣י בִ֑י וְ֝תֻשִׁיָּ֗ה נִדְּחָ֥ה מִמֶּֽנִּי׃

records.literal_gloss: Is it not [that] my help [is] not in me, and success has been driven from me?

en.L: Is [it] not [that] there is no help for me in myself, \q and success has been driven from me?
en.B: Is it not true that I have no help in myself, \q and any hope of success has been driven from me?
en.R: I have nothing left inside me to help myself, \q and every chance of success has been taken from me.

alternatives: Is not my help in me? (a hope)
decisions.reason: The question form with a negative expects agreement: indeed, there is no help left in him.

decisions.choice: success: effective wisdom, resources that work
decisions.reason: Tushiyyah is the word Eliphaz used for what the crafty never achieve (5:12). Job says it has been driven away from him, though he is not crafty.

decisions.choice: a statement instead of a question
decisions.reason: Readable gives the answer the question expects (m1).

source.text: לַמָּ֣ס מֵרֵעֵ֣הוּ חָ֑סֶד וְיִרְאַ֖ת שַׁדַּ֣י יַעֲזֽוֹב׃

records.literal_gloss: To the [one] despairing [is due] from his friend loyalty, and [the] fear of [the] Almighty he forsakes.

en.L: To [the] one in despair [is due] steadfast love from {{gender:their|his}} friend, \q even [if] {{gender:they forsake|he forsakes}} [the] fear of the Almighty.
en.B: Someone in despair should have faithful love from a friend, \q even one who forsakes the fear of the Almighty.
en.R: A friend should show faithful love to someone in despair, \q even if that person no longer honors God All-Powerful.

decisions.choice: the one in despair is owed loyalty, even if he loses his fear of God
alternatives: whoever withholds loyalty from a friend forsakes the fear of the Almighty (a slightly different text)
decisions.reason: The verse is hard. As the Hebrew stands, the one in despair (lammas, "melting away") should receive loyalty from a friend even if he is giving up the fear of God. With a small change of letters ("the one who withholds"), some ancient translations read: whoever withholds loyalty from a friend forsakes the fear of the Almighty. Either way, Job says his friends owe him loyalty and have not given it.
Chesed is the loyal love that people bound to each other owe, here between friends (1 Samuel 20:14-15). Job expected it from his friends.

decisions.choice: the fear of the Almighty: answering Eliphaz
decisions.reason: Eliphaz asked whether Job's fear of God was not his confidence (4:6). Job answers that even if his hold on that fear were slipping, his friends should stand by him.

decisions.choice: the one in despair, his friend: anyone
decisions.reason: The saying is general and applies to any person in despair; Job means himself.
Readable says "honors" for the fear of God, the book-wide choice for this phrase (see 1:1), so the line is not taken as being afraid.

source.text: אַ֭חַי בָּגְד֣וּ כְמוֹ־נָ֑חַל כַּאֲפִ֖יק נְחָלִ֣ים יַעֲבֹֽרוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: My brothers have acted treacherously like a wadi, like [the] channel of wadis [that] pass away,

en.L: My brothers have dealt treacherously like a wadi, \q like [the] channel of wadis [that] pass away,
en.B: My friends have been as undependable as a desert stream, \q like streambeds that run dry,
en.R: My friends have let me down like a stream in the desert, \q like streams that dry up and disappear.

decisions.choice: my brothers: my close companions, the friends
decisions.reason: "Brothers" is used for close companions and allies (2 Samuel 1:26; Psalm 122:8). Job means the three friends who came to comfort him (2:11).

decisions.choice: a wadi: a stream that runs only in the rainy season
decisions.reason: A wadi (nachal) is a valley that fills with rushing water in the rainy season and is dry in summer. A traveler who counts on it for water in the heat finds nothing (Jeremiah 15:18). Verses 15-20 develop the picture.
Bagad is to break faith, to betray a trust (Jeremiah 3:20; Malachi 2:14). The friends failed Job when he most needed them.
Balanced and Readable say "friends", since the men Job means are not his brothers (m1). Literal keeps "brothers".

source.text: הַקֹּדְרִ֥ים מִנִּי־קָ֑רַח עָ֝לֵ֗ימוֹ יִתְעַלֶּם־שָֽׁלֶג׃

records.literal_gloss: the [ones that] are dark from ice, over them hides itself snow.

en.L: which are dark because of ice, \q [and] over which [the] snow hides itself.
en.B: which run dark with ice \q and swell with melting snow.
en.R: In winter they are dark with ice \q and full of melting snow.

decisions.reason: Qoderim, "dark", is the word for the mourners in 5:11. In winter the streams are cloudy with ice and snowmelt.

decisions.choice: hides itself: the snow melts away into them
alternatives: the snow lies hidden under them
decisions.reason: The snow "hides itself" in the streams: it melts into them and disappears, swelling them. Some take it as snow piled over them.
Balanced and Readable say what the hiding is (m2).

source.text: בְּ֭עֵת יְזֹרְב֣וּ נִצְמָ֑תוּ בְּ֝חֻמּ֗וֹ נִדְעֲכ֥וּ מִמְּקוֹמָֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: At [the] time they are scorched they are silenced; when it is hot they are extinguished from their place.

en.L: At [the] time they are scorched, they are silenced; \q when it is hot, they vanish from their place.
en.B: When the heat comes, they fall silent; \q in the hot season they vanish from their beds.
en.R: But when the weather turns hot, they stop flowing; \q in the heat they dry up and are gone.

decisions.choice: they are scorched: they shrink in the heat
decisions.reason: The verb is rare and its meaning is not certain. It seems to mean to be scorched or to shrink; some take it as to flow away. The line says that the streams stop in the dry season.

decisions.choice: silenced, extinguished: the water stops and is gone
decisions.reason: The first verb is to be silenced or destroyed: the noise of the water stops. The second is used of a flame going out (Isaiah 43:17).
"Their place" is the streambed; Balanced says so.

source.text: יִ֭לָּ֣פְתוּ אָרְח֣וֹת דַּרְכָּ֑ם יַעֲל֖וּ בַתֹּ֣הוּ וְיֹאבֵֽדוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: Turn aside [the] caravans of their way; they go up into the wasteland and perish.

en.L: [The] caravans turn aside [from] their way; \q they go up into the wasteland and perish.
en.B: Caravans turn aside from their route; \q they go up into the wasteland and perish.
en.R: Travelers leave their road to look for water; \q they go out into the desert and die.

decisions.reason: 'Orchot can be paths or the caravans that travel them; verse 19 uses the same word for the caravans of Tema. Read as "paths", the verse describes the streams themselves winding off into the desert and vanishing. The caravans, who leave their road to find the water, fit the next two verses best.
Tohu is empty, trackless waste (Genesis 1:2; Deuteronomy 32:10). The travelers who counted on the stream die there.
Readable says why the travelers leave the road, which verses 15-17 and 19-20 make clear.

source.text: הִ֭בִּיטוּ אָרְח֣וֹת תֵּמָ֑א הֲלִיכֹ֥ת שְׁ֝בָ֗א קִוּוּ־לָֽמוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: Look [the] caravans of Tema; [the] travelers of Sheba wait eagerly for them.

en.L: [The] caravans of Tema look; \q [the] travelers of Sheba hope for them.
en.B: The caravans of Tema look for the streams; \q the traveling companies of Sheba hope to find them.
en.R: Traders from Tema look for those streams; \q travelers from Sheba hope to find them.

decisions.choice: Tema and Sheba: trading peoples of Arabia
decisions.reason: Tema was an oasis town in northern Arabia on the caravan routes (Isaiah 21:14; Jeremiah 25:23). Sheba was in southern Arabia, known for its trade (1 Kings 10:1-2); raiders from Sheba took Job's oxen (1:15).
Halikhot are "goings", groups on the move, parallel to the caravans.
Balanced and Readable say what they look for; the Hebrew leaves it to the context.

source.text: בֹּ֥שׁוּ כִּֽי־בָטָ֑ח בָּ֥אוּעָ֝דֶ֗יהָ וַיֶּחְפָּֽרוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: They are put to shame, for he had trusted; they come to it and are dismayed.

en.L: They are put to shame because each had trusted; \q they come to it and are dismayed.
en.B: They are disappointed, because they had been so sure; \q they arrive there and are dismayed.
en.R: They had been sure they would find water, but they are let down; \q they get there and find nothing.

decisions.choice: he trusted: each one of them
decisions.reason: The verb is singular: each traveler had trusted in the stream.

decisions.choice: put to shame: disappointed, their hope failing
decisions.reason: To be put to shame is to have one's trust prove empty (Psalm 22:6; Isaiah 20:5). The friends were the stream Job counted on.
Readable says what the travelers find (m2).

source.text: כִּֽי־עַ֭תָּה הֱיִ֣יתֶם ל֑וֹ תִּֽרְא֥וּ חֲ֝תַ֗ת וַתִּירָֽאוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: For now you have become [like] it; you see a terror and you are afraid.

en.L: For now you have become [like] it; \q you see a terror and are afraid.
en.B: So now you have become like that stream: \q you see something terrible and are afraid.
en.R: And now you have turned out just like those streams. \q You see how terrible things are for me, and you are afraid.

decisions.choice: you have become like it, as the scribes' reading has it
alternatives: you have become nothing (the written form)
you have become so to me (a slightly different text)
decisions.reason: The written consonants (ketiv) read "not": "you have become nothing". The reading the scribes marked (qere) is "to it": you have become like the stream. Some ancient translations read "to me". All three say the friends have failed Job.
Chatat is a rare word for something that causes fear. The friends see Job's condition and back away.
The two verbs sound alike in Hebrew (tir'u, tira'u): what the friends see makes them afraid, perhaps that the same might happen to them, or that they might offend God by taking Job's side.

decisions.choice: how terrible things are for me
decisions.reason: Readable says what the friends see.

source.text: הֲֽכִי־אָ֭מַרְתִּי הָ֣בוּ לִ֑י וּ֝מִכֹּחֲכֶ֗ם שִׁחֲד֥וּ בַעֲדִֽי׃

records.literal_gloss: Have I said, give to me, and from your wealth offer a bribe for me,

en.L: Have I said, "Give to me," \q or, "From your wealth offer a gift for me"?
en.B: Have I ever said, "Give me something," \q or, "Pay a bribe for me out of your wealth"?
en.R: Did I ever ask you to give me anything, \q or to pay money out of your wealth to help me?

decisions.reason: Koach is strength, and also what gives a person strength: wealth and means (Proverbs 5:10).

decisions.choice: offer a gift: pay a bribe or ransom
decisions.reason: Shachad is to give a gift to win someone's favor, often a bribe (Proverbs 17:23). Job never asked the friends to pay anyone to set him free.
Job asked nothing costly of his friends, only loyalty (verse 14). The question runs on through verse 23.
The Hebrew question runs over two verses; Literal and Balanced close it here and let verse 23 carry on with "Or".

source.text: וּמַלְּט֥וּנִי מִיַּד־צָ֑ר וּמִיַּ֖ד עָרִיצִ֣ים תִּפְדּֽוּנִי׃

records.literal_gloss: and rescue me from [the] hand of [the] foe, and from [the] hand of [the] ruthless ransom me?

en.L: Or, "Rescue me from [the] hand of [the] enemy, \q and from [the] hand of [the] ruthless ransom me"?
en.B: Or, "Rescue me from the enemy's hand; \q ransom me from the grip of the ruthless"?
en.R: Did I ask you to save me from my enemies \q or to buy me back from cruel people?

decisions.reason: Padah is the word Eliphaz used of God (5:20). Job did not ask his friends to ransom him; he only asked them to stand by him.
'Aritsim are people who terrify by their power (Psalm 37:35; Isaiah 25:3-5).

decisions.choice: and: the question of verse 22 continues
decisions.reason: The verse continues the list of things Job never asked for.
The Hebrew "and" joins one more thing Job did not say; "Or" makes that clear in a question.

source.text: ה֭וֹרוּנִי וַאֲנִ֣י אַחֲרִ֑ישׁ וּמַה־שָּׁ֝גִ֗יתִי הָבִ֥ינוּ לִֽי׃

records.literal_gloss: Teach me, and I, I will be silent; and what I have erred, make me understand.

en.L: Teach me, and I will be silent; \q and how I have erred, make me understand.
en.B: Teach me, and I will be quiet; \q show me where I have gone wrong.
en.R: Teach me, and I will stop talking; \q help me understand what I have done wrong.

decisions.choice: erred: gone wrong, perhaps without knowing it
decisions.reason: Shagah is to go astray or sin by mistake (Leviticus 4:13; Numbers 15:22). Job is willing to hear of any fault, even one he did not mean.
Eliphaz has hinted that Job is suffering for wrongdoing (4:7-8; 5:17). Job asks him to say plainly what it is.

source.text: מַה־נִּמְרְצ֥וּ אִמְרֵי־יֹ֑שֶׁר וּמַה־יּוֹכִ֖יחַ הוֹכֵ֣חַ מִכֶּֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: How forceful [are] words of uprightness! And what does reproof from you prove?

en.L: How forceful [are] upright words! \q But what does reproving from you prove?
en.B: How forceful honest words can be! \q But what does your arguing prove?
en.R: Honest words can be powerful. \q But what do your arguments prove?

decisions.reason: The verb means to be painful or sharp (1 Kings 2:8; Micah 2:10). Honest words hurt, but they convince. Some read a similar verb, "how sweet" (Psalm 119:103).
Yakach is the language of a law court: to argue, to prove, to correct (5:17). The verb is doubled: "what does your reproving reprove?" The friends' arguments prove nothing.
Readable uses a common word for the force of honest speech (m1).

source.text: הַלְהוֹכַ֣ח מִלִּ֣ים תַּחְשֹׁ֑בוּ וּ֝לְר֗וּחַ אִמְרֵ֥י נֹאָֽשׁ׃

records.literal_gloss: To reprove words do you plan, and to wind [the] words of one despairing?

en.L: Do you plan to reprove words, \q and [treat as] wind [the] words of one in despair?
en.B: Do you mean to correct my words \q and treat the words of someone in despair as wind?
en.R: Do you think you can correct what I say, \q while you treat a desperate person's words as empty wind?

decisions.reason: Ruach here is wind, a picture of words with no weight (8:2; 15:2; 16:3). The friends dismiss Job's words as empty.
No'ash is one who has given up hope (Isaiah 57:10; Jeremiah 2:25). Job asks for allowance for what a desperate man says.
The words to be reproved are Job's own; Balanced and Readable say so.

source.text: אַף־עַל־יָת֥וֹם תַּפִּ֑ילוּ וְ֝תִכְר֗וּ עַל־רֵֽיעֲכֶֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: Even over [the] fatherless you would cast [lots], and you would barter over your friend.

en.L: Even over [the] fatherless you would cast [lots], \q and you would bargain over your friend.
en.B: You would even cast lots for an orphan \q and haggle over the price of your friend.
en.R: You would even throw dice for an orphan \q and make a deal to sell your friend.

decisions.reason: "To make fall" is short for casting lots, as for slaves or plunder (1 Samuel 14:42; Joel 4:3; Nahum 3:10). The friends would gamble even for a fatherless child, the most helpless person there is.

decisions.choice: bargain over: haggle, as in a sale
decisions.reason: Karah 'al is to bargain over something, as traders bargain over goods (Job 40:30).

Yatom is a child without a father to protect him, whom the law and the prophets call God's special care (Deuteronomy 10:18; Psalm 68:6). Job's charge is bitter and exaggerated, but it says his friends treat him as goods, not as a person.
Readable uses a familiar picture of gambling for "cast lots" (m1).

source.text: וְ֭עַתָּה הוֹאִ֣ילוּ פְנוּ־בִ֑י וְעַל־פְּ֝נֵיכֶ֗ם אִם־אֲכַזֵּֽב׃

records.literal_gloss: And now be willing, turn to me; and to your faces, if I will lie.

en.L: And now, be willing [and] turn to me; \q and [I swear] to your faces, if I lie!
en.B: But now, please look at me; \q I will not lie to your face.
en.R: Now please look me in the face. \q I would never lie to you.

decisions.choice: if I lie: an oath, I will surely not lie
decisions.reason: "If I lie" is the first half of an oath whose curse is left unsaid ("may God punish me if ..."), so it means "I certainly will not lie" (1 Samuel 3:17; Job 31).

decisions.choice: turn to me: look at me
decisions.reason: Job asks his friends to look him in the face, not away from him (verse 21).
Balanced and Readable state what the oath means (m1); Literal keeps its form with a bracket.

source.text: שֻֽׁבוּ־נָ֭א אַל־תְּהִ֣י עַוְלָ֑ה וְשׁ֥וּבוּע֝וֹד צִדְקִי־בָֽהּ׃

records.literal_gloss: Turn back, please, let there not be injustice; and turn back, still my righteousness [is] in it.

en.L: Turn back, please; let there be no injustice; \q turn back, my righteousness [is] still in it.
en.B: Think again, please; do not be unjust. \q Think again: I am still in the right in this.
en.R: Please think again and do not be unfair. \q Think again, because I am still in the right.

decisions.choice: and turn back, as the scribes' reading has it
alternatives: and my turning back (the written form)
decisions.reason: The written consonants (ketiv) can be read as a noun, "my return"; the reading the scribes marked (qere) repeats the command "turn back" from the first line. The scribes' reading is followed.

decisions.choice: turn back: reconsider, change your mind
decisions.reason: Shuv is to turn or return; to friends who have turned against Job, it means to think again.

decisions.choice: my righteousness is in it: I am in the right in this matter
alternatives: my righteousness is still in me
decisions.reason: Tsedeq here is the language of a law case: Job is innocent, his case is just. "In it" means in this matter, the dispute between him and his friends.
Balanced and Readable say what turning back means here (m2).
Balanced and Readable express the legal sense (m3), being in the right rather than goodness of character.

source.text: הֲיֵשׁ־בִּלְשׁוֹנִ֥י עַוְלָ֑ה אִם־חִ֝כִּ֗י לֹא־יָבִ֥ין הַוּֽוֹת׃

records.literal_gloss: Is there on my tongue injustice? Or my palate not discern calamities?

en.L: Is there injustice on my tongue? \q Or can my palate not discern calamities?
en.B: Is there anything wrong on my tongue? \q Can my palate not tell what is ruinous?
en.R: Am I saying anything wrong? \q Can I not tell disaster when I taste it?

decisions.reason: The palate tastes food, and so stands for the ability to judge (Job 12:11; 34:3). Job can tell what is happening to him.
Hawwot is the word for calamity in 6:2; it can also mean wicked or destructive speech (Psalm 5:10; 52:4). Job claims both that he speaks no wrong and that he knows his disaster for what it is.

decisions.choice: Can I not tell ... when I taste it
decisions.reason: Readable keeps the picture of tasting but makes Job the subject.
